items.title: Box Breathing (4-4-4-4)
items.body: Used by emergency responders to quickly down-regulate physiological arousal. Inhale deeply through your nose for 4 counts. Hold with lungs comfortably full for 4 counts. Exhale smoothly through your mouth for 4 counts. Hold lungs empty for 4 counts. Repeat for 4 complete cycles.
items.source: Navy SEALs Breath Training & Autonomic Regulation
items.reviewedBy: Dr. Elena Vance, MD (Clinical Pulmonology & Addiction Medicine)

items.title: The 4-7-8 Relaxing Breath
items.body: Developed by Dr. Andrew Weil as a natural tranquilizer for the nervous system. Place your tongue behind your upper teeth. Inhale quietly through your nose for 4 counts. Hold breath for 7 counts. Exhale audibly through your mouth with a whoosh for 8 counts. Repeat 4 times.
items.reviewedBy: Dr. Elena Vance, MD (Clinical Pulmonology & Addiction Medicine)

items.title: Resonant Coherent Breathing
items.body: Breathing at a rate of 5.5 breaths per minute maximizes heart rate variability (HRV) and synchronizes cardiovascular rhythms. Inhale smoothly for 5 seconds, then exhale gently for 5 seconds without pausing. Continue for 3 minutes to restore autonomic balance.
items.reviewedBy: Dr. Elena Vance, MD (Clinical Pulmonology & Addiction Medicine)

items.title: Diaphragmatic Belly Breath
items.body: Place one hand on your chest and one on your belly. Breathe in slowly through your nose, expanding your abdomen like a balloon while keeping your upper chest still. Exhale slowly through pursed lips. This directly stimulates the vagus nerve and shuts down fight-or-flight tension.
items.reviewedBy: Dr. Elena Vance, MD (Clinical Pulmonology & Addiction Medicine)

items.title: 5-4-3-2-1 Sensory Grounding
items.body: Disengage your mind from craving thoughts by anchoring in your five senses. Acknowledge: 5 things you can see around you; 4 things you can physically touch; 3 sounds you can hear; 2 things you can smell; 1 flavor you can taste. This brings you firmly into the present moment.
items.source: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA)
items.reviewedBy: Dr. Elena Vance, MD (Clinical Pulmonology & Addiction Medicine)

items.title: Cold Water Facial Immersion
items.body: Activate the mammalian dive reflex to instantaneously reduce elevated heart rates. Lean over a sink and splash cold water onto your eyes and cheekbones for 15 seconds, or hold an ice cube in your palm. This triggers rapid parasympathetic activation and resets acute agitation.
items.reviewedBy: Dr. Elena Vance, MD (Clinical Pulmonology & Addiction Medicine)

items.title: Progressive Muscle Relaxation
items.body: Beginning at your feet, tense the muscles firmly for 5 seconds, then consciously release for 10 seconds, noticing the sensation of warmth and relaxation. Slowly travel upward through your calves, thighs, abdomen, shoulders, and jaw. Releasing physical tension dissolves urge anxiety.
items.reviewedBy: Dr. Elena Vance, MD (Clinical Pulmonology & Addiction Medicine)

items.title: Tactile Sensory Anchoring
items.body: Keep a textured worry stone, a smooth coin, or a key in your pocket. When a craving produces fidgety hands, hold the object in your dominant hand. Feel the temperature, edges, and weight with intense mindfulness for 90 seconds. Channel motor energy into the anchor.
items.reviewedBy: Dr. Elena Vance, MD (Clinical Pulmonology & Addiction Medicine)

items.title: 3-Minute Urge Surfing Wave
items.body: Close your eyes and visualize your craving as an ocean swell. Rate its intensity from 1 to 10. Locate where the sensation sits in your body—throat, chest, or hands. Breathe into that spot without resisting. Watch the swell reach its peak, flatten, and roll harmlessly onto shore.
items.source: Addiction Research Center, University of Washington
items.reviewedBy: Dr. Elena Vance, MD (Clinical Pulmonology & Addiction Medicine)

items.title: The S.T.O.P. Mental Pause
items.body: When triggered, execute S.T.O.P.: S = Stop what you are doing; T = Take a slow breath; O = Observe your thoughts and emotions without judgment; P = Proceed with an action that aligns with your core health values. This breaks the automatic impulse-action loop.
items.reviewedBy: Dr. Elena Vance, MD (Clinical Pulmonology & Addiction Medicine)

items.title: Cognitive Reality Check
items.body: Say aloud: "I am experiencing an urge to smoke. This urge is a chemical memory, not a command. In 5 minutes it will fade whether I smoke or not. Smoking will not fix my situation; it will only steal my progress." Re-read your core quit reasons on your dashboard.
items.reviewedBy: Dr. Elena Vance, MD (Clinical Pulmonology & Addiction Medicine)

items.title: Compassionate Self-Talk Reset
items.body: Place a warm hand over your heart. Take a slow, kind breath. Silently say to yourself: "This is a moment of discomfort. Discomfort is a natural part of healing. May I be patient with myself. May I remember why I chose freedom." Feel the supportive warmth of your own hand.
items.reviewedBy: Dr. Elena Vance, MD (Clinical Pulmonology & Addiction Medicine)
